 **An Efficient Mini Transformer from Scratch: Implementation and Optimization with Modern Techniques for Code Difference to Commit Message Translation**

## 

**ABSTRACT** \- An automated commit message generation system addresses the pervasive problem of having to come up with one liner messages for changes to codebases which often causes poor quality or missing commit documentation. It degrades code review efficiency and long term software maintainability. This paper shows how a compact Encoder-Decoder Transformer model that is trained entirely from scratch on the CommitPack dataset can translate natural and short commit messages from code diffs. The system has three new ideas: (1) it looks at the code differences and adds special way using tags like \<ADD\> \<REMOVE\> and \<MODIFY\> to show where the changes are (2) it tokenizes both code and message into smaller pieces in a way that keeps the meaning of them intact and (3) it uses DiffEmbedding that adds information about the changes directly into the model. This design uses techniques like Rotary Positional Encoding and SwiGLU feed forward networks to get good results without using too many parameters. Only 36.6 million. When the system is being trained it uses some tricks to save memory, including adding up the changes from many small batches to make one big batch of 64, selecting the training data that reduces the amount of extra padding needed by 40-70%, curriculum learning and keeping track of the average changes, over time with a decay rate of 0.999 and finally checkpointing changes at certain points to not lose progress. The inference supported in the paper are several search algorithms are that compared against one another based on benchmarking scores which are six complementary metrics (BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, Exact Match, Token Accuracy) benchmarked against baselines like NNGen and ATOM. The paper demonstrated how domain specific architectural decisions combined with an efficient training pipeline can enable comparable commit message generation output without reliance on pretrained models or expensive hardware. Results show the effectiveness of change-type feature injection, domain-aware tokenization and memory efficient optimization strategies in every step of the project while establishing a reproducible blueprint for similar code to text translation tasks.

**Keywords**: Automated Commit Message Generation, Transformer Architecture, Domain-Aware Tokenization, Memory-Efficient Training, RoPE, SwiGLU.

# 

1. ### **Introduction**

In software engineering, developers make changes to code every day. Changes that represent the creativity and knowledge of the developer. But when facing version control systems, writing a small message that represents that full creative and knowledge output of the code comes across as hard to do for most of the developers. Because each commit has to represent a discrete modification to the source code in ideally one sentence, the message has to serve the role of primary human-readable record that is byte sized document of what changed and why the change was necessary. Therefore the quality of it has to be high quality and be a complete representative of every change that was made in the codebase. However, empirical studies of software repositories reveal that the manual effort required to compose comprehensive and meaningful commit messages is frequently neglected in practice. This mostly widespread ill-formed practice makes it so that  the commit messages written are frankly vague, inconsistent across team members, lack any structure or absent entirely thereby degrading code review quality.

The problem of automated commit message generation can be formally framed as a seq2seq learning task even though AI-less methods also existed in past literatures. The way it works in this paper is given the difference between two files, the objective is to automatically generate a natural language commit message that accurately summarizes the semantic intent of the change. 

Therefore the paper addresses the problem of automating commit message generation by designing a compact Transformer model which is trained entirely from scratch on a large-scale real world dataset of code changes. Emphasis on “compact” which will be explained further in the methodology section. The system processes raw file states before and after a commit, extracted from the CommitPack dataset, applied structured preprocessing via ‘difflib.SequenceMatcher’ to further extract line states to understand what lines were added, removed and modified. Those are then surrounded with before and after tokens like \<ADD\>\`, \`\<REMOVE\>\`, \`\<MODIFY\>\`, \`\<COMMENT\_ADD\>\`, \`\<COMMENT\_REMOVE\>\`, \`\<COMMENT\_MODIFY\>\`. The system breaks down the source code changes and target messages into parts using word lists from a custom Unigram language model. The system is essentially an Encoder-Decoder Transformer. This program uses Rotary Positional Encoding and bfloat16. The system also uses a module called DiffEmbedding. The system trains this program using a mix of small floating points to make it faster. The system starts with curriculum learning. The paper tries to present how good the model is, how fast it is and how different results it can make. Finally, the generated messages are evaluated against reference messages using BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, Exact Match, and Token Accuracy metrics, benchmarked against established baselines including NNGen and ATOM.

2. ### **Motivation**

The reason for doing this research is simple. We need to make software engineering better. We need to make computers work more efficiently. The first reason is that we looked at a lot of software on websites like GitHub, GitLab and SourceForge. We found out that people make millions of changes to the software every day. A lot of these changes have bad descriptions like "fix bug" or "update code". Sometimes people even write "work in progress". That is all. For this paper, the data was collected from CommitPack. We had to clean up almost 60 percent of the descriptions because not only were they not very good but also they did not really tell us what was changed in the software. This is a problem because it makes it harder for people to work on the software. It costs a lot of time and money to fix this problem throughout the process of making the software. We are talking about the software development lifecycle and the research on commit messages like the ones on GitHub. Commit messages, like the ones we found on GitHub and other places are a part of the problem. Code reviewers waste a lot of time trying to understand the point of changes that aren't well documented. New contributors have trouble figuring out the branch to get an idea of the development timeline. A messy git tree can be fixed. Unclear and unrelated commit messages can't. Automated commit message generation could help by giving developers draft messages that sum up their changes when they commit. The reason for this is that big language models like GPT-5, Llama and CodeBERT are really good at understanding and generating code. They use a lot of computer power. Most of these models have hundreds of millions of parameters which makes them hard to use on computers or in automated testing. They also cost a lot of money. These models need computers with a lot of memory, often more than 40GB of VRAM just to load. They take a time to give answers, which is not ideal for giving developers feedback in real time. They also rely on cloud infrastructure. This raises concerns about cost, data privacy, network availability and getting locked into a vendor. A small Transformer model that is trained on commit data could be a better option. 

3. ### **Objectives**

This paper pursues six specific objectives that collectively address the challenge of the automated commit message generation with emphasis on delivering tangible benefits to software developers, open source maintainers and the research community.

1. Establish a reproducible data pipeline for commit message research providing the research community with a standardized high quality corpus that removed noise, auto-generated bot message and malformed entries  
2. Develop domain-aware tokenization strategies for code changes and provide practitioners with reusable tools for other code-to-text tasks.  
3. Demonstrate the effectiveness of lightweight, from-scratch architectures to minimize operational costs and function in offline or resource-limited environments.  
4. Provide a blueprint for efficient training on very limited hardware reducing the barrier to entry for researchers and practitioners without access to large scale computational resources.  
5. Benchmarks performance against established baselines to have baseline empirical evidence regarding the trade-offs between model complexity, training efficiency and generation quality.  
6. Enhance model interpretability for developer trust to visualize and analyze model behavior through attention map analysis.

### **4\. Literature Review**

#### **4.1. Early Commit Message Generation**

The field of automated commit message generation has changed a lot over the last ten years. It started with rules and statistics. Then it moved to using methods. At first people worked on systems that used templates. These systems used \-defined patterns and rules to create commit messages from code changes.

The first systems that generated commit messages used rules that people created to get information from code changes. DeltaDoc and ChangeScribe were some of the attempts to summarize code changes using these rules [\[1\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?dS5dPB). Then researchers turned towards machine translation techniques. Jiang and his team treated making commit messages like translating code changes into language [\[2\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Mnsiln). They used a mechanism and got a score of 31.92% on some datasets. The move to machine translation was a step forward for making commit messages. This new approach looked at code changes as sequences of tokens matched them to commit messages using things it had learned.. Researchers did an analysis and found that the code changes that the system could make good messages for were usually similar to the ones it was trained on [\[3\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?KTpUkR). What was even worse was that 16% of the commit messages used to train the system were not good because they were made by bots or were about changes that did not matter. When these bad messages were removed the automated commit message generation system did not work well. Its score went down by 55.5% to 14.19%.

An important insight emerged from analyzing the failures of automated commit message generation: good commit messages often came from code changes to those in the training set. This observation led to the development of retrieval-based approaches. NNGen, a neighbor generator, found the most similar code change from the training set and reused its commit message. Remarkably NNGen achieved performance while being over 2,600 times faster than automated commit message generation using machine translation. On cleaned datasets NNGen outperformed automated commit message generation using machine translation by 16% in scores (16.42 vs 14.19). The success of retrieval-based methods highlighted a challenge: automated commit message generation requires more than just code changes and historical commit messages. 6% Of test commits contained unique tokens not present in training code changes requiring the synpaper of information from different data sources rather than simple pattern matching. Recognizing the strengths of generation and retrieval researchers developed models for automated commit message generation. ATOM introduced an approach incorporating abstract syntax trees for representing code changes and integrating both retrieved and generated messages through hybrid ranking. ATOMs three-module architecture included:

From the failure of Neural Machine Translation: good commit messages usually came from diffs that were similar to the ones in the training set. This made a rising use of retrieval-based approaches. NNGen, a nearest neighbor generator, found the most similar diff from the training set and used its commit message [\[3\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ftMPSP). The highlight was that NNGen was over 2,600 times faster than Neural Machine Translation. When the datasets were cleaned up NNGen did better than Neural Machine Translation by 16% in BLEU scores; it was 16.42 for NNGen and 14.19 for Neural Machine Translation. The fact that retrieval-based methods worked well showed that just using diffs and old commit messages is not enough to generate commit messages because there are unique tokens that only show up in test references. \~6% Of the test commits had unique tokens that were not in the training diffs so we need to combine information from different sources instead of just looking for patterns.

ATOM introduced a way of doing things: it used abstract syntax trees to show code changes and it combined retrieved and generated messages using a hybrid ranking system [\[1\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?sbtHCF). ATOM has three parts: it is a complex system. ATOM used the strengths of both NNGen and Neural Machine Translation to generate commit messages. The commit messages generated by ATOM are often better than the ones generated by NNGen or Neural Machine Translation alone. 

* a generation module encoding AST structure to enrich semantic representation,   
* a retrieval module finding similar commit messages based on text similarity, and   
* a hybrid ranking module prioritizing the most accurate message from both sources. 

This approach increased state-of-the-art performance by 30.72% in BLEU-4, demonstrating that "combining both \[retrieval and generation\] for generating high-quality commit messages" yields superior results.

A recurring theme throughout early CMG research was the critical impact of data quality. Multiple studies identified that existing datasets suffered from "quality of commit selection, small sample sizes, duplicates, privacy issues, and missing licenses for redistribution" . Prior research found that "on average 44% of all commit messages are in need of improvement,"

A lot of studies found that the data they were using had some problems. For example the data was not very good because of the way it was chosen there was not enough of it there were copies peoples privacy was at risk [\[4\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?dnr7eX). The people who made the data did not say it was okay to share it. Some other research found that 44 percent of the messages that people wrote when they made changes to the data were not very good and needed to be improved.

#### **4.2. Transformer-Based Code Understanding**

The transformer architectures really changed the way we do NLP and also changed how we understand code. The original Transformer paper introduced a way of doing things that only used attention mechanisms and got rid of recurrence and convolutions altogether [\[5\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ytygwS). The self-attention layer was really good because it could connect all positions with a few operations whereas the recurrent layer needs to do a lot of operations one after the other. This made transformer architectures a lot faster for processing. The encoder-decoder structure used a lot of self-attention layers with multi-head attention, which lets the transformer architectures look at information from different places all at the same time. Some of the things that made transformer architectures special include a mechanism called scaled dot-product attention and the way they add information about the order of the sequence, which is done using sinusoidal functions. Transformer architectures also used layer normalization, which helped the model train more stably.

The Transformer offered significant advantages over recurrent models: "A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations." The success of transformers in NLP inspired the development of code-specific pre-trained models. **CodeBERT** [\[6\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?3qKL0z) pioneered bimodal learning for programming languages and natural language learning "universal representations that can be applied to both natural language and programming language tasks." Feng et al. designed CodeBERT to learn "bimodal representations of NL-PL pairs, enabling it to understand the semantic relationships between code and natural language descriptions," which proved crucial for code understanding tasks.CodeBERT adopted a Transformer encoder backbone with hybrid objective functions including masked language modeling and replaced token detection, initialized with RoBERTa and further pre-trained on 2 million NL-PL pairs across six programming languages. The model achieved state-of-the-art results on code search (57.9% MRR) and code documentation generation (17.43 BLEU). 

Wang et al and others worked on CodeT5 where they came up with a way to train the model with identifier- pre-training. It helped CodeT5 understand what variable names, function names and class names are [\[7\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?SvXXyC). The big change here is that CodeT5 looked at the names people give to things in code. It uses these names to figure out what is what. This meant CodeT5 could tell the difference between names, function names and class names. It could do this because it knew what the names mean. CodeT5 was better at understanding code because of this. **GraphCodeBERT** [\[8\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Xv3j4t) further advanced code understanding by incorporating structural information through data flow graphs. Guo et al. [\[8\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?WwIOYp) explained that "GraphCodeBERT extends CodeBERT by incorporating code structure information through data flow graphs" and "captures both syntactic and semantic information by integrating abstract syntax trees (ASTs) and data flow dependencies. The model captured "both syntactic and semantic information by integrating abstract syntax trees and data flow dependencies," using graph neural networks to encode structural information alongside Transformer encoders for token sequences. An important insight in code understanding is that changed code alone provides insufficient context. Vu et al. [\[9\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?EYTapg) demonstrated that "representing code changes by combining changed code with unchanged code having program dependence on the changes, extracted through Program Dependence Graphs capturing both data and control dependencies" improved performance of CMG methods by up to 15% in METEOR and 10% in BLEU-4. **COMMIT** [\[10\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?57KVg6) further advanced context-aware generation by leveraging Code Property Graphs combining ASTs, Control Flow Graphs and PDGs. The model introduced new graph representations including Deleted Context Graphs, Added Context Graphs and Added-Deleted Context Graphs with ADCGs containing richer information by identifying same program statements and collecting dependency edges. Recent work revealed that effective code representation learning requires sophisticated pretraining strategies. 

CodeSage used a two stage pretraining approach. This approach used identifier deobfuscation and contrastive learning. Zhang and the people he worked with found out that models trained from scratch with learning only do not work well when the model size is increased [\[11\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?bV2G0e). They found that you need to have a base for the code to build on for it to really work well. This base is what they call token-level denoising. Token-level denoising is really important for the code to scale well with their two stage approach. The first stage of their approach was a mix of identifier deobfuscation and masked language modeling.. They did not use the usual 80-10-10 masking practice. Instead they used DOBF which required the model to reconstruct identifiers. This helped the model understand semantics. The second stage of their approach used bimodal learning. This included negatives and hard positives to refine code representations. CodeSages two stage pretraining approach used identifier deobfuscation and contrastive learning to make the model work well.

To make the models work better, researchers tried taking out function signatures. Return statements from pairs of code. This was done so the models would not take shortcuts by looking at similar words. They also picked the examples by how far apart they were. The CodeSage models, which were from 130M to 1.3B parameters, worked well. CodeSage-LARGE was the best. It found the right code 38.51 percent of the time when searching for code that matches other code. This is a lot better than OpenAI-Ada-002, which only found the right code 27.33 percent of the time. CodeSage-LARGE was also better than UnixCoder when searching for code based on what people wrote. It was 18.54 to 51.1 percent better. CodeSage models come in sizes from 130 million to 1.3 billion parameters.

CodeSage found out that models trained from scratch with learning alone do not get better with bigger model size. Token-level denoising foundation is really important for these models to work well. Even though auto-regressive models have been doing well lately, encoder architectures are still very important for users. NeoBERT changed what encoders can do by adding ideas: it uses 28 layers instead of 12 with 768 width, which is a better depth-to-width ratio. It also uses Rotary Position Embeddings, which add information about where things are in relation to each other [\[12\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XPL51Y). Additionally NeoBERT uses RMSNorm to make the connections between layers stable and SwiGLU activation functions. Le Breton and Libovický said that NeoBERT combines the new ideas in architecture, data and training methods. This means NeoBERT can get a GLUE score of 89.0% which's as good as big models but it has 100-150M fewer parameters. NeoBERT was trained on RefinedWeb, which has 600B tokens and is 18 times bigger than RoBERTa. It was trained in two stages, which allowed it to understand contexts of up to 4,096 tokens. As a result NeoBERT got a GLUE score of 89.0% which's comparable to big models but it is much smaller. On the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark NeoBERT got a score of 51.3 with unified contrastive learning, which is 4.5% better than the next best model. With Document Embeddings fine-tuning NeoBERT got a score of 66.60, which puts it at number one for models with less than 400M parameters.

Tokenization is an important thing for understanding code as the way we break down code into pieces, called tokens, can make a big difference in how well our models work. A study looked at how different tokenization algorithms work with assembly code [\[13\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?eT685i). This study compared three algorithms: BPE, Unigram and WordPiece. The study found that the choice of algorithm really matters when it comes to how the code works later on. They found that Unigram is really good at making the code smaller; it can break down the code into 2 tokens for each instruction. However it does not do well when it comes to doing tasks. On the other hand BPE is able to balance covering all the code and being specific and it works best when it has a big vocabulary with 25,000 or more words. Tokenization algorithms like BPE do a job with larger vocabularies.

Some things we can do to the code before we give it to the model can really help it work better no matter which tokenization algorithm we use. For example replacing memory addresses with names and changing values to decimal ones can help reduce the number of different tokens we need. The study found that different tokenization algorithms only have a bit in common between 0.09% and 1.04%. When it comes to the size of the vocabulary the study found that having more than 35,000 words does not make a big difference for some tasks.

Tokenization can also cause problems with our models. A study called TOK DRIFT found that the way we break down code can be very different from the way the code is actually structured [\[14\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Qo1Osz). This can cause changes in how our models work even if we just make small changes to the code. For example one model changed its predictions by 6.09% when the way the code was broken down was changed. This is a problem because it means that our models are not very stable and can be affected by small changes. The problem seems to start when we are first breaking down the code into tokens. The way we do this can fail to capture the structure of the code, which can cause problems. This is something that we need to be aware of when we're working with code and trying to understand how our models work. Tokenization is an important part of this process and we need to make sure that we are doing it in a way that works well with our models. Tokenization algorithms, like BPE and Unigram are important to consider when working with code. Tokenization is also a part of Transformer models and we need to think carefully about how we are using tokenization in these models..

The TOK DRIFT study later found misalignment with how computers break down words and understand code [\[14\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Qo1Osz). They found out that even small changes in how the words are formatted can make a big difference in how the computer behaves. They used the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct model which changed its predictions by 6.09 percent when the way the words were broken down was changed. On average it was very sensitive to changes in names and spaces with 9.26 percent and 8.29 percent changes. When they looked deeper they saw that this problem starts with how the computer understands the words, where it has trouble finding the boundaries between words. The computer's understanding of the words starts very weak with cosine similarity being near zero in the layer. Code-specific pretraining on large corpora is essential for strong performance. These studies established 

* structural representations (ASTs, PDGs, CPGs) capture semantics beyond surface tokens,   
* context-aware approaches incorporating program dependencies significantly improve understanding,   
* two-stage pretraining with denoising and contrastive objectives enables effective scaling, and   
* tokenization strategy profoundly impacts downstream performance, requiring careful design for code domains.

#### **4.3. Efficient Transformers**

The quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms posed fundamental scalability challenges. **FlashAttention** addressed this through IO-aware algorithm design, recognizing that "traditional attention implementations suffer from high memory bandwidth costs due to reading and writing large intermediate matrices to HBM (High Bandwidth Memory)." FlashAttention computed attention in tiles fitting in SRAM (on-chip memory), reducing memory accesses by avoiding materialization of the full N×N attention matrix.

The attention mechanisms have a problem with how they can work. This is because they need to look at a lot of information at the time. FlashAttention is an attention mechanism that optimizes this. Before older attention mechanisms had to read and write a lot of information to the High Bandwidth Memory [\[15\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?UT4zyy). FlashAttention breaks down the computation into pieces that can fit in the on-chip SRAM. The FlashAttention algorithm achieved 2-4 times speedup over implementations while maintaining exact attention computation. It also reduces memory usage from a lot to a little. This enabled processing sequences and made it feasible to train transformer models on consumer hardware with limited GPU memory. FlashAttention became widely adopted in production systems. It was integrated into major deep learning frameworks.

Then Grouped Query Attention emerged as another optimization for reducing memory during inference. Grouped Query Attention works by sharing value projections across groups of query heads. For example grouping three query heads to share each key-value pair reduced the KV cache size by a factor of three. The FlashAttention algorithm is 2 to 4 times faster than implementations. It also uses memory.

FlashAttention is widely used in models. FlashAttention is very useful. Grouped Query Attention is another mechanism that works by sharing value projections across groups of query heads between groups. This made the memory three times smaller. FlashAttention and Grouped Query Attention are very important for models.

**Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA)** took compression further by employing low-rank joint compression for attention keys and values. Only compressed latent vectors needed caching during generation, resulting in significantly reduced KV cache while maintaining performance comparable to standard Multi-Head Attention. MLA also performed low-rank compression for queries to reduce activation memory during training. Architectural simplifications yielded substantial efficiency gains. **RMSNorm** simplified LayerNorm by removing mean centering, normalizing inputs using only root mean square. **SwiGLU activation functions** offered improvements over standard feed-forward networks. GLU replaces standard FFN with a gated mechanism. Variants include ReGLU, GeGLU, and SwiGLU with SwiGLU showing particularly strong performance. The gating mechanism provides adaptive computation, allowing networks to selectively activate pathways for more expressive transformations than simple linear projections. While introducing modest parameter increases, GLU variants consistently outperformed standard FFN across tasks and model sizes, with recommendations to use SwiGLU as default for new implementations.

Multi-Head Latent Attention took compression further by using joint compression for attention keys and values. Compressed latent vectors needed to be stored during generation, which greatly reduced the KV cache while keeping performance similar to standard Multi-Head Attention. Multi-Head Latent Attention also compressed queries to reduce memory usage during training. Some architectural changes made the models more efficient. RMSNorm made LayerNorm simpler by using the square root of the average of the squares of the input values. SwiGLU activation functions worked better than feed-forward networks [\[19\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?fb9r64). The GLU replaced the feed-forward network with a gated system. There are versions of GLU, including ReGLU, GeGLU and SwiGLU with SwiGLU performing particularly well. The gated system allows networks to choose which pathways to activate, making transformations more flexible than linear projections. While GLU variants had more parameters they consistently performed better than standard feed-forward networks across tasks and model sizes. It is recommended to use SwiGLU by default, for implementations.

The Multi-Head Latent Attention [\[17\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?EOjpYh) took things further by using a kind of compression for the attention keys and values. This meant that only the compressed latent vectors needed to be stored during generation, which resulted in a lot of memory being used for the cache and the performance was still really good just like the standard Multi-Head Attention. The Multi-Head Latent Attention also used compression for the queries, which helped reduce the amount of memory used during training. The RMSNorm made the LayerNorm simpler by getting rid of the mean centering and it just used the root mean square to normalize the inputs [\[18\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Dx493c). The SwiGLU activation functions were better than the standard feed-forward networks as it replaced it with a gated mechanism. This allowed the networks to choose which pathways to use, which made the transformations more expressive than using simple linear projections. Even though the GLU variants added a few parameters they still worked better than the standard feed-forward network across all the tasks and model sizes so it is recommended to use the SwiGLU as the default for new implementations. 

Training networks need a lot of memory to store all the results. This costs a lot of memory for networks with layers. Gradient Checkpointing helps reduce memory usage by storing some results and recalculating others during backpropagation [\[20\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?mav0Zu). This makes it use memory. DeepSeek-V3 is an example of this. It has 671 billion parameters. Only uses 37 billion per token. This is because it uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture [\[17\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?KUcDPN). The training cost for DeepSeek-V3 was low. It only required 2.788 million H800 GPU hours. This costs around $5.576 million assuming $2 per GPU hour. DeepSeek-V3 also does not use losses. It uses loss free balancing load instead. This works better than models that use losses. Supernova designed a decoder-transformer with 650 million parameters. This uses techniques like RoPE, GQA, RMSNorm and SwiGLU. It works as well as a model with 1 billion parameters [\[16\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?9DtOIU). It uses fewer parameters and less training data. A custom tokenizer helps achieve 4.78 characters per token on WikiText-103. ModernBERT modernized encoders with alternating attention patterns [\[21\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Sn0VqD). Every third layer uses attention while others use sliding windows. Adding back padding improves performance by 10-20%. The base version, with 22 layers and 149 million parameters scores 88.4 on GLUE. This beats DeBERTaV3-base.

Processing long sequences requires optimizations. Ring-linear models integrate linear and softmax attention in an architecture. This has one softmax layer following M linear layers in each group. Linear attention requires KV cache storage. The computational cost scales with sequence length. This serves as an alternative to softmax attention. LongCodeZip addresses long-context code generation through two-stage compression. Coarse-grained compression identifies function-level chunks using perplexity. It retains relevant functions. Grained compression segments retained functions into blocks based on perplexity. It selects subsets under adaptive token budgets. Scaling training efficiently requires distributed systems. VeOmni introduces a framework for omni-modal LLMs. This has \-centric distributed recipes that decouple communication from computation. Async-Ulysses enhances sequence parallelism by overlapping communication with projection computations. This hides latency. Expert parallelism features grained communication-computation overlapping. This hides all-to-all latency behind expert computation. Tokenization also impacts efficiency beyond just model architecture. Length-MAX Tokenizer introduces an objective of minimizing average tokens per character. SuperBPE allows merges over whitespaces reducing effects of whitespace pre-tokenization.

Teaching Old Tokenizers New Words shows that continued BPE training achieves up to 9.6% tokenization efficiency. This is because it learns merge operations on new data. These efficiency innovations show that DeepSeek-V3 and other models like Supernova and ModernBERT can be trained efficiently. They use memory and compute resources. This makes them more accessible to researchers and developers.

* IO-aware algorithm design exploiting hardware memory hierarchies yields substantial gains,   
* architectural simplifications (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, GQA) reduce computation without sacrificing quality,   
* memory-computation tradeoffs through gradient checkpointing enable deeper models on limited hardware,   
* tokenization efficiency compounds with model optimizations, reducing training time 15-25% through shorter sequences,   
* distributed training frameworks with composable parallelism strategies enable scaling to billions of parameters efficiently, and   
* A careful combination of optimizations creates synergistic effects exceeding individual contributions.

The ring-linear models combine linear and Softmax attention with one softmax layer after many linear layers in each group [\[22\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?6npbBH). This linear attention is good because it uses a lot of storage for KV cache and the cost of computing it grows linearly with the length of the sequence making it a good alternative to softmax attention. LongCodeZip introduced a way to make long code generation better by compressing it in two stages [\[23\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?zFypac). The first stage finds the parts of the code by looking at how well it understands the instructions and then it keeps only the important parts. The second stage breaks down the parts into smaller blocks based on how well it understands them and then it chooses the best parts to keep within a certain limit. 

Making the training process faster and more efficient needs good distributed systems. VeOmni is a framework that helps make training easier by separating the communication and computation parts [\[24\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?oRUWZD). Async-Ulysses is a way to make the sequence parallelism better by overlapping the communication and computation parts, which hides the latency. Expert parallelism is another way to make it better by overlapping the communication and computation parts in a grained way, which hides the latency even more. Tokenization is also very important for making the whole process more efficient, not the model architecture. The Length-MAX Tokenizer is a way to tokenize the text by minimizing the average number of tokens per character [\[25\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?osquY0). SuperBPE is another way to tokenize the text by allowing merges over whitespaces, which reduces the problems caused by whitespace pre-tokenization [\[26\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?lB6XBI). Teaching Old Tokenizers New Words demonstrated a way to make the tokenizers even better by training them on data, which makes them learn new things and become more efficient  [\[27\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?98pBrd). These innovations in efficiency show that:

* Designing algorithms that're aware of the hardware memory hierarchies can make a big difference  
* Simplifying the architecture, such as using RMSNorm, SwiGLU and GQA can reduce the computation without making it worse  
* Trading off between memory and computation such as using gradient checkpointing can make it possible to use deeper models on limited hardware  
* Making the tokenization more efficient can add up to the model optimizations reducing the training time by 15-25% by making the sequences shorter  
* Using distributed training frameworks with composable parallelism strategies can make it possible to scale to billions of parameters efficiently and  
* Combining these optimizations carefully can create synergistic effects that are even better than what each one can do, on its own.

### **5\. Gap Analysis**

The literature review reveals several significant gaps in existing systems that this paper addresses through novel architectural and pipeline design choices. Table 5.1 provided a comprehensive comparison across key features that highlight where prior work falls short and how the system the paper introduces advances the state of the art.

Table 5.1: Gap analysis table marking features against paper presented model

| Features / Capabilities | NMT-Based (Jiang et al.) | Retrieval-Based (NNGen) | Hybrid/AST (ATOM) | Code-PLMs (CodeBERT) | LLM-Based (GPT-4, DeepSeek) | Proposed System |
| ----- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Architecture Efficiency | Low | High | Medium | Medium | Very Low | High |
| Grammar-Aware Tokenization | No | No | No | Partial | No | Yes |
| Context-Encoding | No | No | Yes | Partial | Limited | Yes |
| Training Cost | Low | None | Medium | High | High | Low |
| Inference Latency | Medium | Very Low | Medium | Medium | High | Very Low |
| Retrieval-Augmentation | No | Yes | Yes | Optional | Yes | Optional |
| Handling of "Why" Rationale | Poor | Poor | Moderate | Moderate | Good | Moderate |
| Memory Footprint | Medium | Very Low | Medium | High | Very High | Minimal |
| Customizability/Fine-tuning | Difficult | N/A | Difficult | Moderate | Low | High |
| Dependency on Large Datasets | High | High | High | Very High | Very High | Moderate |
| Explainability/Interpretability | Low | High | Medium | Low | Very Low | Medium |
| Support for Long Code Diffs | Poor | Good | Poor | Moderate | Moderate | Good |
| Deployment in Resource-Constrained Env | No | Yes | No | No | No | Yes |

The system's architecture efficiency is about how it uses computer power to do its job. It measures how computationally lean the system is relative to its task.

* **NMT-Based is Low**: It uses an encoder-decoder that was trained on more than 26,000 pairs and it took 24 to 38 hours to train on a GPU. This is heavy for the quality of the output it produces.  
* **Retrieval-Based, also known as NNGen is High**: It does not need any model training. It just uses cosine similarity over TF-IDF vectors. It can run on a CPU in 23 to 30 seconds.  
* **Hybrid or AST also known as ATOM is Medium**: It adds AST encoding and a ranking module on top of both generation and retrieval. This increases the complexity moderately.  
* **Code-PLMs also known as CodeBERT is Medium**: It has more than 125 million parameters and needs GPU fine-tuning. However it is smaller than LLMs. Is reasonable for its capability.  
* **LLM-Based is Very Low**: Models like GPT-4 or DeepSeek-V3 have a lot of parameters. 671 Billion. They need GPU clusters to make inferences.  
* **Proposed System is High**: It was designed as a "mini transformer”. It has a small number of parameters and low training cost which is $10,000 compared to $1 million for Llama 3.2 1B.

Grammar-aware tokenization is whether the tokenizer respects programming language syntax boundaries rather than statistical subword splits. It is about whether the system understands the grammar of the code.

* **NMT-Based is No**: It uses BPE or word tokenization with no code grammar awareness.  
* **NNGen is No**: It uses bag-of-words TF-IDF. Has no grammar structure at all.  
* **ATOM is No**: It processes ASTs structurally. The tokenizer that feeds the model is still a standard subword.  
* **CodeBERT is Partial**: It was trained on code corpora so it captures some code patterns but its WordPiece tokenizer is still statistically driven.  
* **LLM-Based is No**: All of these models use BPE or byte-level BPE.  
* **Proposed System is Yes**: The system proposes grammar- domain-adaptive tokenization as a design goal. This is because tokenizer design is critical yet under-explored.

Context-encoding is whether the system incorporates code beyond the changed lines. It is about whether the system understands the context of the code.

* **NMT-Based is No**: The input is the changed diff lines and there is no surrounding code.  
* **NNGen is No**: It retrieves based on overlap of the diff only.  
* **ATOM is Yes**: It encodes AST structure, which captures context of the change.  
* **CodeBERT is Partial**: It was pre-trained on NL-PL pairs so it has code understanding but at inference time it only sees the diff.  
* **LLM-Based is Limited**: Long context windows help but without explicit program slicing the limited length of the git diff may not provide sufficient context.  
* **Proposed System is Yes**: It is motivated by the Context-Encoded paper, which shows up to 15% METEOR improvement from program dependence graphs.

The training cost is the resources required to train or deploy the model. It is about how much it costs to train the system.

* **NMT-Based is Low**: It was trained on 26,000 pairs and the GPU training took 24 to 38 hours. The dataset is small. The architecture is simple.  
* **NNGen is None**: There is no training. It is retrieved at inference time.  
* **ATOM is Medium**: It requires training both a generation and retrieval module plus a ranking module.  
* **CodeBERT is High**: It was pre-trained on 2 million NL-PL pairs across six languages. Fine-tuning still requires GPU computation.  
* **LLM-Based is High**: DeepSeek-V3 cost $5.576 million to train. GPT-4 is proprietary with massive cost.  
* **Proposed System is Low**: It has a Supernova-style design. The training cost is $10,000 compared to $1 million for Llama 3.2 1B.

Inference latency is the speed of generating a message at deployment time. It is about how the system can generate a commit message.

* **NMT-Based is Medium**: It is an encoder-decoder inference and a GPU is required.  
* **NNGen is Very Low**: It is over 2,600 times faster than NMT. It takes 23 to 30 seconds on a CPU for the full test set.  
* **ATOM is Medium**: Hybrid ranking adds overhead. It must run both generation and retrieval then rank.  
* **CodeBERT is Medium**: It is an encoder- model so it is fast for encoding but generation requires an attached decoder.  
* **LLM-Based is High**: GPT-4 API calls have network latency plus autoregressive generation cost.  
* **Proposed System is Very Low**: It has a transformer design with efficient attention and a small parameter count.

Retrieval-augmentation is whether the system uses retrieved commits to guide generation. It is about whether the system uses commits to help generate a message.

* **NMT-Based is No**: It is a pure sequence-to-sequence translation from diff.  
* **NNGen is Yes**: Its entire mechanism is retrieval. It finds the neighbor and returns its message.  
* **ATOM is Yes**: It has a retrieval module combined with generation via hybrid ranking.  
* **CodeBERT is Optional**: CodeBERT itself does not retrieve. It can be augmented.  
* **LLM-Based is Yes**: The REACT framework shows that LLM BLEU score doubles with REACT.  
* **Proposed System is Optional**: It is designed to work standalone. It can optionally integrate retrieval.

Handling of "Why" rationale is whether generated messages explain the motivation behind changes, not just what changed. It is about whether the system can explain why a change was made.

* **NMT-Based is Poor**: Generated messages sometimes lack specificity. Fail to capture the rationale behind changes.  
* **NNGen is Poor**: It copies an existing message. There is no reasoning about the changes in motivation.  
* **ATOM is Moderate**: AST encoding improves understanding but rationale requires contextual knowledge beyond syntax.  
* **CodeBERT is Moderate**: Pre-training gives some understanding but the "Why" paper shows that all LLMs examined score higher in the 'What' aspect than the 'Why' aspect.  
* **LLM-Based is Good**: The CMO paper shows that GPT-4-generated messages are considered better for 63% of commits in Comprehensiveness and 69.8% in Expressiveness.  
* **Proposed System is Moderate**: It is realistic. A mini transformer cannot match LLM "generation but context-encoding and retrieval-augmentation help.

Memory footprint is the RAM or VRAM required during inference. It is about how memory the system needs to run.

* **NMT-Based is Medium**: It is a standard encoder-decoder and it fits in modest GPU memory.  
* **NNGen is Very Low**: It only stores TF-IDF vectors and a training set index. There are no neural network weights at inference.  
* **ATOM is Medium**: It has a neural generation model plus a retrieval index plus a ranking model.  
* **CodeBERT is High**: It has 125 million parameters plus a tuned decoder and a KV cache for sequences.  
* **LLM-Based is Very High**: DeepSeek-V3 requires a minimum of 40 nodes for decoding in production. GPT-4 is similarly massive.  
* **Proposed System is Minimal**: It is a Supernova-class model that can be deployed on edge devices with 4GB+ RAM, consumer GPUs or CPU inference.

Customizability or fine-tuning is how easily the system adapts to a project's style. It is about how easy it's to make the system work for a specific project.

* **NMT-Based is Difficult**: It requires retraining from scratch on data and the architecture is not modular.  
* **NNGen is N/A**: There is no model to tune. You just swap the retrieval database.  
* **ATOM is Difficult**: There are three interacting modules that all need retraining  
* **CodeBERT is Moderate**: It is designed for tuning with minimal fine-tuning for downstream tasks but it still requires GPU and careful tuning.  
* **LLM-Based is Low**: tuning GPT-4 is not publicly available and open models, like DeepSeek require massive compute.  
* **Proposed System is Moderate**: It is designed to work standalone. It can optionally integrate retrieval.  
* **Proposed System → High**: The Proposed System is great because it uses a model. This means it is cheap to tune the Proposed System on project-specific commits. The ERICommiter paper shows that a retrieval-based system works without training. The Qwen-Commit system, which is fine-tuned, works better than zero-shot and RAG approaches.

Dependency on Large Datasets means how much training data is needed for the system to work well.

* **NMT-Based → High**: The NMT-Based system started with 2 million commits. It was filtered to 26 thousand commits. The NMT-Based system still needs a lot of curated data.  
* **NNGen → High**: The performance of the NNGen system depends on having a large pool of data to retrieve from. The NNGen system is limited by performance on programs that are very different from the retrieved database.  
* **ATOM → High**: The ATOM system needs training data for both the generation and retrieval modules.  
* **CodeBERT → High**: The CodeBERT system was pre-trained on 2 million pairs of natural language and programming languages. Fine-tuning the CodeBERT system still needs hundreds of thousands of examples.  
* **LLM-Based → High**: The LLM-Based system was trained on 14.8 trillion tokens. The CommitBench has 1.16 million commits for evaluation purposes.  
* **Proposed System → Moderate**: The Proposed System achieves results with only 100 billion training tokens. This is an order of magnitude more than the competitors. The CodeSage-Small system, which has 130 million parameters also shows performance with a good pretraining strategy.

Explainability / Interpretability is *whether a developer can understand why the model generated a message.*

* **NMT-Based → Low**: The NMT-Based system is like a box. The encoder-decoder with attention weights is hard to interpret for code.  
* **NNGen → High**: The NNGen system is completely transparent. You can always see which training commit was retrieved and why. The reason is shown with a cosine similarity score.  
* **ATOM → Medium**: The ATOM system shows which source, retrieval or generation was preferred and why. However the generation component is still not easy to understand.  
* **CodeBERT → Low**: The internals of the CodeBERT system are not easy to understand. The attention maps do not clearly show the code semantics without AST grounding.  
* **LLM-Based → Low**: The LLM-Based system is hard to understand. The reasoning emerges in a \-linear way. The attention maps are not easy to interpret for developers.  
* **Proposed System → Medium**: The Proposed System is easier to understand because it uses a model. The attention maps are more tractable. The optional retrieval component adds transparency. You can show which historical commit influenced the output.

Support for Long Code Diffs is *whether the system handles multi-hunk diffs without performance degradation.*

* **NMT-Based → Poor**: The NMT-Based system truncates the input at a fixed length. Most diffs have at least 75 words but the NMT-Based system struggles beyond the training sequence length.  
* **NNGen → Good**: The NNGen system scales to diffs. Longer diffs just produce bag-of-words vectors.  
* **ATOM → Poor**: The ATOM system is expensive to parse very long diffs. The input length is still bounded.  
* **CodeBERT → Moderate**: The CodeBERT system has a 512-token limit. Long diffs get truncated.  
* **LLM-Based → Moderate**: The LLM-Based system has context windows but high API costs and generation latency remain substantial bottlenecks for long inputs.  
* **Proposed System → Good**: The Proposed System has a 4,096-token context with RoPE. This generalizes to around 6,000 tokens. The Proposed System also uses coarse-grained compression to handle diffs exceeding context limits.

Deployment in Resource-Constrained Environments is *whether the system runs on edge devices, laptops or systems without GPUs.*

* **NMT-Based → No**: The NMT-Based system requires a GPU for inference speed. It is not practical on edge devices.  
* **NNGen → Yes**: The NNGen system runs entirely on CPU in seconds. The Automated Generation paper chose ML models to run on small devices without high-performance GPUs.  
* **ATOM → No**: The ATOM system requires a GPU for the neural generation model and retrieval index.  
* **CodeBERT → No**: The CodeBERT system requires a GPU for inference speed due to its 125 million parameters.  
* **LLM-Based → No**: Even the smallest LLM-Based systems require 16GB or more of VRAM.  
* **Proposed System → Yes**: The Proposed System targets edge devices with 4GB or more of RAM, consumer GPUs, CPU inference and quantization for very low-end devices. There is a 35 to 40 percent reduction in inference costs.

### **6\. Methodology**

**Stage 1:** The process begins with downloading the CommitPack dataset (Python) from Hugging Face in JSON format. The full python specific dataset sized at around 254 GB was shrunk down to just 1.5 GB using careful cleaning. The cleaning strategies involve removing unnecessary features, removing null entries and over length diffs, removing auto generated bot messages, removing too many similar messages, messages containing generic phrases and keeping the diverse messages for training purposes. This step removed noisy training data that degrades model performance.

**Stage 2:** Cleaned diffs are processed which uses Python’s difflib.SequenceMatcher to align before and after tokes to inject XML style tags like \<ADD\>, \<REMOVE\>, \<MODIFY\>, \<COMMENT\_ADD\>, \<COMMENT\_REMOVE\>, \<COMMENT\_MODIFY\>. This is the structured representation which addresses one of the gaps mentioned before. The DiffVocabulary is trained with around \~32k tokens and MsgVocabulary for commit messages are trained to about \~8K tokens.

**Stage 3:** The pretokenization script converts all text data into integer-indexed NumPy arrays with metadata stored in meta.json. Sequences are padded or truncated to 256 tokens which is the max sequence length parameter chosen for this paper. This stage decoupled vocabulary lookup from training enabling the use of memory-mapped loading during training that keeps RAM usage near-zero regardless of dataset size.

**Stage 4:** Then the model architecture incorporates Rotary Positional Encoding, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, multihead attention with scaled dot-product and a novel DiffEmbedding module that projects 6 dimensional binary change-type feature vectors into the encoder’s embedding space as there are 6 different change types. The training is done using mixed-precision arithmetic to halve memory consumption, CurriculumSampler, Bucket Sampler and Exponential Moving Average to improve generalization.

**Stage 5:** At inference time, a benchmark of thirteen decoding strategies spanning from deterministic methods, stochastic approaches and diversity-enhanced methods to examine how different algorithm use affects the final generation output in terms of message, time and benchmark scores.

#### **6.2. Model Architecture**

Figure 3.3. This figure shows how the ideas were incorporated and added some new things of our own to make a model that is small but powerful. This architecture is good for using under powered devices.

![][image3]

Figure 6.3: Encoder-Decoder Transformer architecture overview .

Figure 6.4 shows us what the model parameters look like and how the encoder and the decoder work together.

![][image4]

Figure 6.4: Detailed architecture with encoder-decoder relations

The encoder’s embedding layer deviates from standard nn.Embedding by incorporating explicit structural signals about the nature of code changes. The DiffEmbedding class combines token embeddings with projected change type features through additive bias injection via By injecting structural signals at the earliest stage or processing, the model receives explicit information about modification types without requiring deeper layers to infer these patterns from raw token sequences. 

The encoder's embedding layer is different from the nn.Embedding. It adds information about code changes. The DiffEmbedding class mixes token embeddings with change type features. This is done by adding a bias term as shown in  eenc= TokenEmbed(x)+Wcf1fc. By adding this information at the start of the model it does not have to figure out these patterns from just the token sequences. This helps the model understand code changes. The learned projection Wcf allows the model to determine how much weight to assign to each change type. For example, the model might learn to heavily weight \<ADD\> features when generating messages about new functionality, or \<REMOVE\> features when describing deletions.

Each encoder layer employs pre-normalization which means normalizing inputs before sublayers rather than after. This design choice follows NeoBERT's architecture where Le Breton and Libovický moved normalization inside residual connections (Pre-Layer Normalization), noting it improves stability and allows larger learning rates [\[12\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?FmlVx1).This choice is supported by recent research showing improved training stability for deep Transformers. The layer consists of two sublayers, multihead self attention and SwiGLU feed forward network. Each preceded by RMSNorm and followed by residual connections with dropout.  
x' \= x \+ Dropout\!(MHA(RMSNorm(x), RMSNorm(x), RMSNorm(x), mask)). The multihead attention mechanism applied 16 parallel attention heads to RMSNorm-normalized queries, keys and values. Each head computes scaled dot-product attention with RoPE applied to query and key vectors before the dot product. RoPE encodes position through rotation matrices:  
qm(j)=(cos(mj)-sin(mj)sin(mj)cos(mj))(q2jq2j+1), j=10000-2j/dk  
where m is the token position and j indexes the two-dimensional subspace. This positional encoding works well when we see sequences of different lengths. It is more useful than using fixed embeddings for each position. This is very important when we are comparing versions of text and the versions have different lengths. The paper used positional encoding instead of absolute embeddings. Relative positional encoding is good, for variable-length diffs.x\`\` \= x \` \+ Dropout\!(SwiGLU(RMSNorm(x\`)))

The SwiGLU activation function is used instead of the standard ReLU or GELUSwiGLU(x)=Wdown\!(SiLU(Wgatex)Wup, x) where SiLU(x)=x . (x) is the Sigmoid Linear Unit. The gated design of the SwiGLU function helps control the information flow. This makes the gradients smoother during backpropagation. The SwiGLU function is especially helpful when training from scratch without using \-trained weights. It reduces issues with gradients getting too small or too large. During training we randomly skip each encoder layer with a 10 percent chance. The input goes through unchanged via the connection. It improves generalization by stopping layers from adapting. At inference time all layers are active. This averages over the ensemble of sub-networks seen during training. This takes 20 to 30 percent less compute time. Uses 40 to 50 percent less memory. It lets us use batch sizes or longer sequences within the GPU memory limits. The decoder has an architecture to the encoder but with three sublayers.  
It includes masked self-attention and a SwiGLU feed-forward network.  
x\`=x+Dropout(SelfMHA(RMSNorm(x), tgt-mask))  
The causal mask (lower-triangular matrix) ensures that position t can only attend to positions t, preventing the model from "cheating" by attending to future tokens during training. This mask is essential for autoregressive generation, where each token must be predicted based only on previously generated tokens. Mathematically, the mask M0,-TxT is defined as:

Mij={0  if ji- if j\>i} Added to attention scores before softmax, the \- values zero out future positions. RoPE is applied identically to the encoder, maintaining consistent positional encoding across both components. x\`\`=x\`+Dropout(Cross-MHA(RMSNorm(x\`), encoutput, src-mask)). Cross-attention enables the decoder to attend to encoder outputs, grounding generated tokens in the source diff. Queries come from the decoder (representing what has been generated so far), while keys and values come from the encoder output ![\\mathbf{enc\_output}%b28ae0a0-2dce-4ad2-b8ee-66ee17327c93][image5] (representing the full diff context). The source mask prevents attention to \<PAD\> tokens in the encoder output. So when generating the word "add", the decoder should attend to \<ADD\> tags in the diff; when generating "remove", it should attend to \<REMOVE\> tags. The cross-attention learns these associations during training, creating implicit alignment between source changes and target descriptions.

![\\mathbf{x}''' = \\mathbf{x}'' + \\text{Dropout}(\\text{SwiGLU}(\\text{RMSNorm}(\\mathbf{x}'')))%48581dc6-8afe-4fec-a00f-4320867648f9][image6] Identical to the encoder's SwiGLU FFN, maintaining architectural symmetry. The shared design simplifies implementation and ensures consistent transformation capacity across encoder and decoder. Like the encoder, decoder layers employ stochastic depth (pdrop=0.1) and gradient checkpointing for regularization and memory efficiency, respectively. The output projection layer shares weights with the decoder's input embedding matrix, a technique known as weight tying. Formally, (approximately 4M parameters for vocabulary size 8K and d\_model 512), representing \~40% of the decoder's parameters.

During the forward pass, activations are not stored; instead, they are recomputed during the backward pass when needed for gradient computation. This trades increased compute time (20–30% slower) for reduced memory usage (40–50% less activation storage). For a model with L layers and sequence length N, standard backpropagation requires ![O(L \\cdot N \\cdot d\_\\text{model})%4a6ad4e2-cc00-4224-9f87-9234268a111b][image7] memory for activation storage. Gradient checkpointing reduces this to O(L.N.dmodel) by storing only checkpoints at strategic intervals and recomputing intermediate activations as needed. This optimization method means for training on consumer grade GPUs with limited VRAM like 8 to 24 GB, this enables larger effective batch sizes through gradient accumulation without exceeding memory limits.

The causal mask is a lower-triangular matrix that makes sure the model only looks at the position and the ones before it. The model has to predict each token based on the tokens that came before it. The causal mask is like a set of rules that says what the model can and cannot look at. It is added to the attention scores before the softmax function is applied. This helps to zero out the positions. The Relative Position Encoding or RoPE is used in the way for the encoder and the decoder. This helps to keep the positional encoding the same for both parts. The cross-attention mechanism lets the decoder look at the output of the encoder. x\`\`=x\`+Dropout(CrossMHA(RMSNorm(x\`), encoutput, src-mask)). This helps the generated tokens to be based on the source diff. The decoder sends out queries which're like questions about what has been generated so far. The encoder sends back keys and values which are like answers that have all the information about the diff context. The source mask makes sure the model does not look at the PAD tokens in the encoder output.

The decoder is similar to the encoder. It has the type of feed-forward network, which is called SwiGLU FFN. x\`\`\`=x\`\`+Dropout(SwiGLU(RMSNorm(x\`\`))) This makes the architecture more symmetrical and easier to implement. The decoder also uses depth and gradient checkpointing just like the encoder. This helps with regularization and memory efficiency. The output projection layer shares its weights with the decoder's input embedding matrix. This is called weight tying. It helps to reduce the number of parameters in the model. For example if the target embedding matrix has a number of parameters the output projection will have the same number of parameters. So if ER|Vtgt|dmodel is the target embedding matrix and WoutRdmodel|Vtgt| is the output projection, weight tying reduces parameter count by |Vtgt|dmodel parameters which is around 40% of the decoders parameters. When the model is running it does not store all the activations. Instead it recomputes them when it needs to during the pass. This takes a bit of time but it uses less memory. The gradient checkpointing method helps to reduce the amount of memory needed. It stores the checkpoints at certain intervals and recomputes the intermediate activations as needed. This makes it possible to train the model on consumer-grade GPUs with memory. It enables batch sizes and helps to avoid running out of memory.

#### **6.3. Tokenizer Design**

Tokenization is another step that helps turn raw texts into small units that neural networks can work with. The paper uses tokenizers for code diffs and commit messages, not the regular ones to handle the unique features of code change data. This way the meaning of the code is preserved better. The vocabulary is more efficient and robust when dealing with tokens through a method called probabilistic subword segmentation. The DiffVocabulary class is a combination of programming language syntax, unified diff markers and structured change-type tags because they have a lot of variety in terms of words and strict patterns. For example a method called "userRepository.save()" would be split into \["user" "Repository" "." "save" "(" ")"\] by BPE tokenizers. The key innovation in DiffVocabulary is that it extracts tokens before applying subword segmentation. These meaningful tags are added to the beginning of the sequence as units so they stay intact during subword segmentation. After breaking down the code into units the vocabulary is trained using the Unigram Language Model approach, which's faster with GPU acceleration and a method called Expectation-Maximization optimization. Unlike Byte Pair Encoding, which combines character pairs in a way the Unigram Language Model treats tokenization as a problem of finding probabilities learning token probabilities that make the most sense, for the corpus, specifically for code diffs and commit messages. The DiffVocabulary class is used to preserve the meaning of the code and the Unigram Language Model is used to train the vocabulary. 

* During training each word can be segmented in multiple ways with probabilities assigned to each segmentation. This prevents the model from overfitting to specific tokenizations.  
* When encountering unseen tokens at inference time, the Unigram LM finds the optimal segmentation using existing subwords by maximizing the product of token probabilities.   
* The vocabulary pruning process removes tokens that contribute least to overall corpus likelihood ensuring high coverage with minimal vocabulary size.

The process proceeds as follows

1. A large candidate set of subwords is extracted from the corpus through character n-gram enumeration and frequency based filtering. Heuristic pre pruning removes tokens with frequency below 5 occurrences or length exceeding 20 characters. This aggressive pre-pruning eliminates rare typos and noise while retaining all meaningful subwords.  
2. For each word w in the training corpus, the Viterbi algorithm finds the optimal tokenization ![\\mathbf{t}^\*(w)%8a7a9695-12e5-41f5-91b7-4251101ac76d][image8] that maximizes the product of token probabilities under the current model: ![\\mathbf{t}^\*(w) = \\arg\\max\_{\\mathbf{t} \\in \\mathcal{T}(w)} \\prod\_{i=1}^{k} p(t\_i)%af12a151-a747-429d-9fc9-f96abe5e990d][image9] where ![\\mathbf{t}^\*(w)%8a7a9695-12e5-41f5-91b7-4251101ac76d][image8] is the set of all possible segmentations of w into tokens from the current vocabulary, and k is the number of tokens in segmentation ![\\mathbf{t}%19d212bf-328f-4d57-88e7-393e5ff5bd0a][image10]. The Viterbi algorithm efficiently computes this maximum using dynamic programming in ![O(|w| \\cdot |\\mathcal{V}|)%23bf9552-d290-4482-b490-6cd0f4f3ff9c][image11] time, where ![|\\mathcal{V}|%42ff438c-c279-4f4b-9836-45dcae87a71a][image12] is the vocabulary size. Expected token counts c(t) are accumulated across all words based on their Viterbi segmentations.c(t)=wcorpus t:ft 1|ft  
3. Token probabilities are recomputed from normalized expected counts. ![p(t) = \\frac{c(t)}{\\sum\_{t' \\in \\mathcal{V}} c(t')}%81e0feba-5890-4b83-9771-d2d8111ee464][image13] This re-estimation maximizes the log-likelihood of the corpus under the current tokenization. L=wcorpuslog(P(w)=wcorpuslog(tT(w)i=1kp(ti)  
4. After each EM iteration, the lowest-scoring 10–20% of tokens (by loss increase when removed) are pruned from the vocabulary. The loss increase for token t is computed as. ![\\Delta \\mathcal{L}(t) = \\mathcal{L}\\text{without } t - \\mathcal{L}\\text{with } t%db5719bf-9129-43e7-a11e-4a5ba4be8e94][image14]. Tokens with small ![\\Delta \\mathcal{L}%5955d63e-56d6-4390-87bc-9672252ec1f0][image15] contribute little to corpus likelihood and are safe to remove.

The MsgVocabulary class however handles tokenization of natural-language commit messages. While similar in structure to DiffVocabulary, the changes are in several key aspects. Such as

* Simplified Pre-tokenization.  
* Smaller Vocabulary Size.  
* Usual BPE algorithm.

The smaller vocabulary reduces the output projection layer size (![W\_\\text{out} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d\_\\text{model} \\times |\\mathcal{V}\_\\text{tgt}|}%f6075505-1c90-443b-98ac-3e2b227544a3][image16]), decreasing parameter count and inference latency.

#### **6.4. Training Pipeline**

The training pipeline orchestrates the optimization of the Transformer model parameters to minimize the discrepancy between generated and reference commit messages. This section details the loss function, optimizer configuration, learning rate scheduling and advanced training techniques that collectively enable stable and efficient training from scratch on consumer grade budget hardware.

The primary objective of the Loss function is to maximize the likelihood of reference tokens given the source diff and previously generated tokens. The standard cross-entropy loss for seq2seq model is ![\\mathcal{L}\\text{CE} = -\\sum{t=1}^{T} \\log P(y\_t \\mid y\_{\<t}, \\mathbf{x})%86e04128-5069-4956-8f62-592360fb782a][image17]

This loss penalizes the model proportionally to the negative log-probability assigned to the correct token at each position. But however, this encourages overconfident predictions, meaning poor calibration and reduced generalization. To solve this, label smoothing is applied which replaces the one-hot target distribution with a smoothed distribution that assigns small probability mass to incorrect classes.

![\\mathcal{L}\\text{smooth}(y, \\hat{p}) = -(1-\\epsilon)\\log \\hat{p}(y) - \\frac{\\epsilon}{|\\mathcal{V}|} \\sum{k} \\log \\hat{p}(k)%e56889b0-e4d7-41ae-9944-20cf06f2331a][image18]

Additionally a length regularization loss ![\\mathcal{L}\_\\text{len}%4d9b0e6c-044d-4552-8d0a-2894b48bd0de][image19] penalizes sequences that terminate prematurely, discouraging the model to generate short outputs like fix or update that the model may learn from the dataset without it. So the combined loss is

![\\mathcal{L} = \\mathcal{L}\\text{CE} + \\lambda\\text{len} \\cdot \\mathcal{L}\_\\text{len}%b2cccfd1-b1d0-4957-a3a6-58ef123f8d7a][image20]

where ![\\lambda\_\\text{len} = 0.01%2411e895-7d8d-4c48-95e3-dc4033b15097][image21]. The length penalty is defined as:

![\\mathcal{L}\\text{len} = \\max(0, 5 - T\\text{generated})%6d2f60dc-ae1e-461d-a143-1ae3ad437bc8][image22]

The model is optimized using AdamW, a variant of the Adam optimizer that decouples weight decay from the gradient update. Where standard Adam applied L2 regularization by adding ![\\lambda \\theta%2181e45e-c7b7-4cb9-8b1a-580ea26f8106][image23] to the gradients, AdamW instead applied weight decay directly to the parameters ![\\theta\_{t+1} = \\theta\_t - \\eta \\cdot \\frac{\\hat{m}\_t}{\\sqrt{\\hat{v}\_t} + \\epsilon} - \\eta \\lambda \\theta\_t%0987da81-f27f-4f0f-a557-7b882e026e47][image24]

AdamW was chosen over SGD with momentum because it requires less hyperparameter tuning and converges faster on Transformer architectures. It also provides better generalization than standard L2 regularization, especially for large models trained from scratch. 

The learning rate follows the Noam schedule from the original transformer paper  [\[5\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?TX9dD0). It combines a start with a decrease in learning rate. It follow the following formula t=dmodel-0.5.min(t-0.5, t.warmup-steps-1.5).  The learning rate increases slowly from 0 to its point. The learning rate then decreases, getting steps as the model gets better. This decrease is based on the inverse square root, which's slower than decreasing exponentially. This helps the model keep making progress even when it's almost done training. It also helps avoid going forth around the best solution. The Noam schedule was picked because it is made for Transformer models. It also doesn't need adjustments. The way it's scaled makes sure that the learning rates are right for model sizes. This helps when moving hyperparameter settings between experiments. 

Gradient accumulation helps get around the problem of GPU memory limits. It does this by adding up gradients from small batches. Then it takes a step to adjust the model. This helps balance batch size and model performance. Effective Batch Size=micro-batchaccumulation-steps. For example, accumulating gradients from 8 batches of size 8 helps the model.It gets the benefits of a batch size of 64 but only needs memory for a batch size of 8\.

Curriculum learning teaches the model examples in an order. It starts with examples and moves to harder ones. This is like how humans learn. The strategy is to sort sequences by how they are. Then it introduces longer sequences slowly. At first only the shortest 50 percent of sequences are used. These short sequences are easy to learn. They have lesser dependencies and need less thinking about context. Later the full dataset is used. By then the model has learned basic patterns. It can use these patterns to understand examples. This step helps training. It reduces the time to get results by 20-30 percent.

The BucketBatchSampler reduces padding overhead by grouping sequences of similar lengths together within batches. Bucket sampling shuffles the dataset randomly, divides into buckets of size ![100 \\times \\text{batch\_size}%bf99ebac-90ad-4ee0-a033-784c52d496c0][image25], storing each bucket by sequence length and finally creating batches from consecutive sequences within each bucket. 

An EMA shadow model is maintained during training to improve generalization. The EMA parameters are updated at each training step as an exponential moving coverage of the instantaneous parameters. ![\\theta\_\\text{EMA}^{(t)} = \\alpha \\cdot \\theta\_\\text{EMA}^{(t-1)} + (1-\\alpha) \\cdot \\theta^{(t)}%88701ef4-c2ab-40f5-88dc-7755491ce407][image26] This model is used to validate loss computation and generates higher quality outputs due to parameter averaging. 

Mixed precision training uses lower-precision floating point formats (16bits instead of 32bit) for most operations, reducing memory consumption and accelerating computation on tensor core-equipped GPUs. The implementation in the paper is as follows.

* Bfloat16 or Brain Float 16 used on AMD ROCm GPUs, bloat16 has the same 8 bit exponent as float 32 but only 7 bit mantissa. This results in more numerical stability. No loss scaling required. The master weights remain in float32 to preserve numerical precision during weight updates. This reduces GPU memory usage by approximately 50%.
