#### **6.5. Inference**

When the trained model is used it creates commit messages one token at a time. This makes it really important to have a decoding strategy to get good output. The evaluation framework tests several decoding strategies. These strategies fall into three groups: methods that always do the thing, methods that try different things and methods that try to make the output more varied. By comparing all these strategies we can see how they balance quality, speed and diversity. The methods that always do the thing include search algorithms like

* Greedy decoding is a method that selects the token with the probability at each step. This method uses the vocabulary, generated tokens and the encoded source information yt=argmaxvVP(v|y\<t, x).   
* Beam search is another method that keeps a number of candidate sequences at each step. It tries to add all next tokens to each candidate and then keeps the top ones based on their cumulative log probability. The scoring function uses the log probability with a length penalty that only applies to completed sequences. The sequence length and the length penalty exponent are important here lp(y)=(5+|y|)n(5+1)n score(y)=t=1|y|logP(yt|y\<t, x)lp(y) .  
* There are also sampling methods like Top-k sampling. This method only lets you choose from the k probable tokens at each step. Then it picks one based on their probabilities. We can try values for k, such as k=50 for more variety or k=20 for better quality.  
* Top-p sampling is a method that selects a set of tokens based on their probability. It picks the set of tokens that exceeds a certain threshold and then it chooses one from this set. Vp={v1,...,vk}, where k=min{j:i=1jP(vi)p}  
* Pure temperature sampling is a method that adjusts the softmax temperature. It does not use any filtering by PT(v)=exp(logP(v)/T)v\`Vexp(log(P(v\`)/T)  
* Typical sampling is a method that chooses tokens based on how surprising they're. It filters out tokens that're too predictable or too surprising. The model sorts the tokens, by their surprise value. Then pick the smallest set that exceeds a certain threshold. H(y\<t)=-vVP(v|y\<t,x)logP(v|y\<t, x), surprise(v)=|logP(v|y\<t, x)-H(y\<t)|  
* Min-p sampling is a method that filters out tokens based on their probability. It only keeps tokens that have a fraction of the top tokens probability. For example if we set min\_p=0.05 the model will only keep tokens that have at least 5% of the top tokens probability. Vminp=v:P(v|y\<t,x)minp.maxv\`P(v\`|y\<t, x)

Then finally the Diversity-Enhanced methods such as

* Diverse beam search (Vijayakumar et al., 2016\) partitions the beam into G groups, each exploring different regions of the search space. At each timestep, groups are processed sequentially, and diversity penalties discourage selecting tokens chosen by earlier groups.s\`tg(v)=stg(v)-g\`\<g1\[v=ytg\`\] where ![s^g\_t(v)%3bf9b87b-032b-4d4c-94fb-2618f2eb71fe][image28] is the original score for token v in group g at step t, ![y^{g'}\_{t}%0e3f99a4-6503-4e01-b1a0-5dc66ed67fdd][image29] is the token selected by group g' at the current step, and ![\\lambda=0.5%bc560b21-f6c5-409d-8c25-28223532f245][image30] is the diversity penalty. Configuration uses 6 beams divided into 3 groups of 2 beams each.  
* Contrastive search (Su et al., 2022\) balances prediction confidence against degeneracy penalty by comparing candidate hidden states to previously generated hidden statesscore(vj)=(1-).log(P(vj|y\<t, x)-.max1itcos(ht+1(j),hi) where ![h\_{t+1}^{(j)}%ddde112a-04b0-4485-aef3-6cd79f031fb1][image31] is the decoder hidden state after selecting candidate ![v\_j%12ef765c-c993-4a1e-99d4-5378ff56d61f][image32], ![h\_i%f234e077-febe-4778-b1a9-b4de728b00c9][image33] are previous hidden states, and alpha=0.6 controls the trade-off. Configuration uses top-k=4 candidates.  
* Diversity Beam Search with MMR Reranking. After generating k candidates via standard beam search, each candidate c is rescored as. MMR(c)= . Relevance(c)-(1-).maxsSSimilarity(c,s) where text similarity is computed as Similarity(c,s)=|bigrams(c)bigrams(s)||bigrams(c)bigrams(s)|. Additionally, a repetition penalty discourages repeated n-grams within a single sequence by dividing the probability of previously generated tokens by a penalty factor. ![P\_\\text{adjusted}(v) = \\begin{cases} P(v) / \\text{penalty} & \\text{if } v \\text{ appeared in last } n \\text{ tokens} \\ P(v) & \\text{otherwise} \\end{cases}%7d0b6fe5-bc37-409a-b5f1-cc34fa0f104f][image34]

### **7\. Testing and Evaluation/Performance/ Comparative Analysis**

Six metrics were used to assess generation quality. Each metric captures a part of output accuracy.

* BLEU-4 is a way to see how similar the messages that the system generates are to the reference messages. It looks for sequences of four words that're the same in both messages. If the score is higher that means the messages are more similar. The score can be anywhere from 0 to 100%.  
* METEOR is another way to measure how well the system generates messages. It tries to find a balance between precision and recall. It uses something called WordNet to find words that're similar but not exactly the same. METEOR looks at the reference words. Tries to match them exactly or by looking at the stem of the word or by finding synonyms. This makes METEOR really good at understanding ways of saying the same thing.  
* ROUGE-L is a measure of how the system generates messages that are similar to the reference messages. It looks at the sentences and the order of the words. It tries to balance precision and recall.  
* Exact Match is a way to measure how many of the generated messages are the same as the reference messages. This is not case sensitive so it does not matter if the words are in lower case. It also ignores spaces. This metric shows how well the system can generate messages that are perfect. In life it is very rare for messages to match exactly because people use language in so many different ways.. It gives us an idea of how well the system can do at its best.  
* Token Accuracy is a way to measure how the generated tokens or words match the reference tokens. It does this by comparing each token one by one. For example it checks if the first word generated is the same as the word, in the reference message. Then it looks at all the matches. Averages them out. This helps us see where the model is making mistakes. We can see if the model has trouble at the start or the end of the message. By looking at the accuracy we can see where the model needs to be improved.

| PtrGNCMsg | 2019 | 12.64% | 8.25 | 13.40 | Pointer-Generator | Handles OOV words |
| CoRec | 2021 | 7.62% | 4.42 | 8.73 | Hybrid (Ret+Gen) | Context-aware retrieval |
| RACE | 2022 | 19.90% | 10.52 | 18.53 | Retrieval-Augmented | Exemplar-guided generation |
| CodeBERT-CMG | 2020 | 11.86% | 6.30 | 12.78 | Pre-trained Encoder | Code-specific pretraining |
| ATOM | 2020 | 10.51% | **18.51** | **22.02** | AST \+ Hybrid Rank | Structural code representation |
| COME\* | 2023 | \~25.07% | \~21.48 | \~31.97 | CodeT5 Fine-tuned | Best traditional CMG approach |
| CCT5\* | 2023 | \~15.96% | \~14.26 | \~24.33 | T5 Pre-trained | Code change-oriented model |
| GPT-3.5-Turbo | 2023 | 26.15% | 18.80 | 18.27 | LLM (Zero-shot) | Current SOTA |

**7.2 Training Curves**

![][image40]

Figure 7.2: Training and validation loss curves showing loss over steps.

The Noam scheduler has a warmup phase that lasts for the 4000 steps. During this time you can see that the loss goes up at first. Then it comes down really fast. After the warmup phase is over the inverse square root decay helps the Noam scheduler converge. When the Noam scheduler starts with the epochs it uses short sequences. The Noam scheduler is able to reduce the loss during these initial epochs. The way the Noam scheduler does this is similar to how other big models like NeoBERT,'re trained. The NeoBERT model was trained in two stages. First it was trained on sequences and then it was trained on longer sequences. The NeoBERT model started with sequences that were 1,024 tokens long. Then it was trained on sequences that were 4,096 tokens long. Noam scheduler also used gradient checkpointing to make the training process more efficient. This technique helps reduce the amount of memory needed from O(n) to O(√n). This means that the Noam scheduler can be made deeper with more hardware constraints [\[12\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?vIEKvV).

### **8\. Results and Discussion**

The model was tested with 13 decoding algorithms on a set of 100 code changes and their corresponding commit messages. To evaluate its performance we used metrics like BLEU-4, METEOR and ROUGE-L F1. We also looked at how it took to generate output and how long the output was. This helped us get a picture of what the model can do. However as Zeng and others noted in their study metrics like BLEU are not very good at measuring the quality of the generated text. They often do not match what humans think is good or bad. This is especially true when the reference messages are not very good. Trigui and Al-Khatib said we need ways to evaluate models. Schall and others created a benchmark called CommitBench. It helps filter out low-quality data and has over 1.6 million code changes and messages from 72,000 GitHub repositories [\[4\], \[29\], \[30\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Qp9Q1n). Our model got a BLEU-4 score of 0.0522 or 5.22% with a search method. This means it has some overlap with human-written commit messages. This is good because it shows the model can generate text that sounds natural and uses phrases. It did this without being trained on an amount of code. Compared to models ours did not do as well. Some models that retrieve examples or were trained on amounts of data did better. Our model learned from a smaller dataset specific to the task. The good news is that our model is efficient and can be used in real-world applications. It has the potential to be useful, in practice. The model was efficient. The model can be deployed in applications. The model performed well with metrics.

### **9\. Future Work**

We are working on making our system better at understanding code. One way to do this is by using something called tuning on pre-trained code models. We can use models like CodeBERT, StarCoder or CodeT5 [\[6\], \[7\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ylrgi2). These models have already learned a lot about code from billions of lines so they can help our system understand code better. We just need to make sure the pre-trained encoder can handle the input we have which includes change-type tags. If we do this our system can get a lot better at handling diffs. Still generate text efficiently. We can also make the system look at tokens at once like 512 or 1024 using Flash Attention [\[15\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?61cPyw). It uses memory so we can look at pieces of code without running out of space. Dao et al. Showed that Flash Attention is way faster than the way of doing things and it still gets the same results. This means our system can handle diffs without cutting them off and it can understand the context of multi-file commits.

Another thing we can do is add information about the code structure like function definitions and class hierarchies to the encoder. This is called syntax tree or AST node embeddings [\[8\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?KD5PA4). The AST can help our system understand the code better because it includes information that's not in the text-only diffs. Guo et al. Showed that using ASTs and data flow graphs can really improve how well the system understands code. We can use a graph network to encode the AST. Then combine it with the token embeddings in DiffEmbedding. This will help our system understand how different parts of the code are related.

We can also train a model to score how good the commit messages are, based on what developers think. Then we can use this model to tune the generation model so it produces commit messages. This is called reinforcement learning. It has been used to make language models. We can use it to make our system produce commit messages that're more informative, concise , grammatically correct and accurate [\[29\]](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?o9mywD). This way we are optimizing for what humans think is good, not surface-level metrics.

We can make a plugin for VS Code or JetBrains IDE that suggests commit messages when the user's about to commit some changes. The plugin can show the suggested commit messages in the message editor and let the user accept, reject or regenerate them. We can also collect feedback from the users like whether they accepted or edited the suggested commit message to make the system better. This will help us improve our system and make it more useful for developers.

### **10\. Limitation**

The system has some limitations that affect how well the system works and how useful the system is. The model is not very big. The model was made from scratch. The model has a count of layers and parameters than other models like CodeBERT and GPT-2. This means the model is not very good at understanding changes that require an understanding of the language. The model is good at changes but the model struggles with bigger changes that involve many files and lines of code. The system is limited because the model is not very good at handling changes. The model works with small changes but the model has trouble with changes that are too big for the model to understand.. 

* The words the model knows are decided when it is trained. They do not change. If the model sees a word or a new programming term that it does not know it will not be able to understand it very well.  
* The model can only look at a number of lines of code at a time. If a change involves lines of code the model will not be able to see the whole change. For instance if someone is changing a database the model might not be able to see all the changes because they are too big.  
* The model was only tested on commit messages in English. It probably will not work well on messages in other languages.  
* The model has a time understanding what kind of change is being made. It can tell if something was added or removed. It does not know what the change means or which specific lines of code were changed.  
* The model only looks at the text of the code. It does not understand the structure of the code. This means it can miss relationships between different parts of the code.  
* The model generates its words instead of copying them from the original code. This can lead to mistakes where the model generates a word that sounds good but is not correct. If the model could copy words from the code it would make fewer mistakes and be more accurate.  
* The model has trouble with changes that involve lines of code or many files. It is better at changes that only involve a few lines of code.

The system limitations are important because they affect how well the model works and how useful it is. The model is good at some things. It is not very good at other things. For example the model is good at changes but it struggles with bigger changes. The model limitations are the system limitations and the system limitations are the model limitations. The model and the system are the thing and they have the same limitations. The system limitations and the model limitations are important because they affect how well the system works and how useful it is.

### **11\. Conclusion**

This paper is about a system that generates commit messages automatically. The system uses a kind of model called an Encoder-Decoder Transformer model. This model was trained from the beginning using the CommitPack dataset. The problem this system solves is that software developers waste a lot of time writing good commit messages that describe code changes correctly. When commit messages are bad or missing it is hard to review the code, find mistakes and maintain it over time. The Encoder-Decoder Transformer model is a part of the system. It uses ideas to work well and is small enough to run on regular computers. The model was trained in a way. This way of training lets it work on computers that do not have the best graphics cards. The system can generate commit messages in ways. This means you can choose between speed and quality. To see how well the system works a standard method called beam search was used. The model did well with scores of 0.0522 BLEU-4, 4.91 METEOR and 6.45 ROUGE-L F1. These scores are better than a model from 2018 called NNGen. Not as good as a model from 2020 called ATOM. Looking at all the evaluation metrics the model is good at understanding the meaning of the code changes. However the model needs to get better at handling changes. The evaluation metrics used include BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, Exact Match and Token Accuracy. These metrics give a picture of how well the model works. The model is very good at similarity according to BERTScore. It also shows areas that need to be improved such as handling \-change diffs. The CommitPack dataset and the Encoder-Decoder Transformer model are parts of the system. The system and the Encoder-Decoder Transformer model can be used to generate commit messages.
